claims.text: Alloying a transition-metal catalyst with a secondary metal can shift the surface d-band center.
The surface d-band center governs catalytic activity and selectivity by controlling adsorption energies of key reaction intermediates.
A pure transition-metal catalyst has an intrinsic electronic structure and pristine surface characteristics.
Secondary-metal alloying alters the local electronic structure of the catalyst.
A shift in the d-band center adjusts the adsorption strengths of key intermediates.
An optimal intermediate d-band-center position enhances turnover frequency by balancing adsorption and desorption energetics.
An optimal intermediate d-band-center position improves product selectivity by balancing adsorption and desorption energetics.
Deviations from the optimal d-band-center position may impair catalytic performance.
An alloyed catalyst will exhibit higher catalytic activity than the pure catalyst if alloying places the d-band center at an optimal intermediate position.
An alloyed catalyst will exhibit improved product selectivity relative to the pure catalyst if alloying places the d-band center at an optimal intermediate position.
The proposed relationship applies primarily to reactions whose performance is governed by adsorption energetics.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold under moderate conditions that preserve catalyst structure.
The proposed relationship may fail when sintering or phase transitions change the catalyst structure.
Prior evidence supports a correlation between d-band-center shifts and catalytic performance.
The quantitative relationship between d-band-center position and performance varies with the reaction and catalyst system.
XPS or UPS can be used to determine the catalyst's d-band-center position.
